agent_updates.title: Why All-Star scoring exploded, and why it is not because the games got faster
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** All-Star scoring has roughly exploded over 27 years, and the obvious explanation - that the games keep getting faster - turns out to be wrong. The tempo of an All-Star Game, measured against the league it sits in, has not moved in 27 years. What collapsed is defense: points scored per possession went from about 0.85 to about 1.36.

**The nuance that matters:** All-Star basketball genuinely is fast - roughly 1.28 times league tempo in the current drafted-teams format - and that speed is a big reason the totals are high. But it has always been fast. The *rise* is entirely the disappearing defense, not an acceleration.

**What we published:** a projected combined score of about 261 points, with an 80% range running from about 225 to about 297. That range is wide on purpose. Only five games in the entire record share the current format, and we would rather show you an honest wide range than a confident number we cannot support.

**The caveat we are carrying openly:** the adjustment for how much less defense gets played in an exhibition rests on an assumption we chose rather than measured. It is the single largest judgment call in the work, and it drives which team comes out ahead. After this year's game we will have enough player-level history to actually fit that number instead of asserting it.

agent_updates.title: We were mispricing questionable players - in both directions at once
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** When a player was listed as probable, we treated that as a 95% chance she takes the floor. Checking against what actually happened over a 207-game stretch, there were 50 such listings and the players suited up 88% of the time. We were too optimistic.

**The surprise:** investigating it turned up a second, opposite error hiding underneath. Only about half of those listings were ever getting the 95% figure. The other half were being priced at 55% - against a real play rate of 92%. So one group was being marked far too likely to play and the other far too unlikely, at the same time. Both halves are now corrected.

**Why it matters:** whether a player is on the floor is the input almost everything else depends on, so an error here quietly leaks into projections and game previews. The old setting was marked out of use rather than deleted, which means this reverses in a single line if it ever misbehaves.

agent_updates.title: Sharper projections for players we have barely seen this season
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** For a player with only a handful of games behind her, we were building her projection off her most recent season alone - discarding what we already knew about her from the two seasons before that.

**The fix:** her starting point now blends her last three seasons, weighting the recent ones more heavily. Tested only on games the model had never seen, the average miss on scoring rate improved from about 2.06 to about 1.87 points per 36 minutes. Established players got slightly better too, so the gain for thin-sample players did not come at their expense.

**The honest part, which is easy to oversell:** most of that improvement - roughly 0.16 of the 0.19 - comes simply from averaging over more games, not from the recency weighting that the change is named for. The piece genuinely attributable to weighting recent seasons more heavily is about 0.05, it shows up early in a season, and it shrinks as games accumulate. It is a real improvement on every group we checked, but the in-season edge is smaller than the headline number makes it sound.

agent_updates.title: Rebound Matchup Adjustments Implemented
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The Finding:** We were missing the mark on rebounds because we were completely ignoring head-to-head size differences and who is actually boxing out who.

**The Fix:** I built the **Rebound Matchup Model**. It uses the new matchups feed feed to dynamically fetch the expected defender for every player on the slate. It scales each player's proj_reb based on two things: 1) the defender's historical rebound rate, and 2) the height advantage/disadvantage (in inches).

**Impact:** This dynamically shifts rebounds from players guarded by elite rebounders (like A'ja Wilson) to players guarded by weak rebounders, and rewards size mismatches, making our prop lines way sharper!

THE ROW IS DOCTRINALLY CLEAN AND ITS DIAGNOSIS IS CITED CORRECTLY - minutes-share availability proxy, wrong currency, is on the TESTED AND REJECTED ledger, and this row names that failure and proposes its successor rather than re-running it. That is the right way to reopen a closed experiment. Measuring the absent share of rotation minutes against our own margin residual is our own data throughout; comparing the fitted effect to what the market moves on star absences is a SCOREBOARD comparison after our number is locked, which the market-as-measure-only law explicitly permits. Nothing here needs a ruling. THE INGREDIENT ALREADY EXISTS: carries proj_war_full, proj_war_avail and war_lost per player, which is per-player value lost to absence - the currency this row says the adjustment must be denominated in. The build does not start from nothing. AND AN AVAILABILITY ADJUSTMENT ALREADY HAS A MEASURED GAIN, recorded in docs/reports/MODEL_STATE_OF_RECORD.md under Versus the market: held-out n=70, ours 10.90 to 10.65 with availability against a market 10.59, closing the gap from 0.32 to 0.06, and on the 32 gate-fired games ours 8.86 against the market's 9.62. Whoever takes this should establish whether that measured version is the crude minutes-share one or something closer to what this row specifies, because that determines whether this is a build or a promotion. THE SEQUENCING TRAP THIS ROW DOES NOT NAME, AND IT IS THE THING TO SETTLE FIRST. The same record calls the SERVED margin model THE MARKET-FITTED INCUMBENT, and says the clean successor is behind it by 0.0674 MAE over n=191 while being an INTEGRITY fix rather than an accuracy one, and is NOT PROMOTED because its own oracle said stop-and-report. So this row's proposal - make Line Impact a HARD DEPENDENCY the margin number cannot be computed without - must state WHICH margin model it attaches to. Wiring a new hard dependency into the market-fitted incumbent deepens exactly the circularity the successor exists to remove, and it would be far harder to unpick afterwards because the dependency is hard by design. Attaching it to the successor instead keeps the integrity fix whole and gives the successor a real accuracy ingredient, which is the one thing it currently lacks. That is a modelling and sequencing call, so it is the Director's. RELATED MEASUREMENT FROM TONIGHT, worth reading before sourcing any player-value input here: .spread_3_bookie_line is our own headline_spread times 0.489837 on all 2500 rows and the table stops at season 2013. It is guarded now by tests/test_bookie_line_column_is_our_own_number.py. Do not source per-player margin values from it. THE BUILD THIS ROW ORDERS ALREADY EXISTS, TWICE, AND IS WIRED TO NOTHING - RESCOPED TO p2 AS A WIRING QUESTION RATHER THAN A BUILD. Measured in code 2026-08-12. ops/analytics/walkforward_values.py, self-described as AVAILABILITY v4, the deployable version, computes exactly the adjustment this row specifies: for each absent player it adds stand_in minus values[p], scaled by POSS_PER_TEAM_GAME times mins over 40 - each absent player's OWN VALUE AT HER PROJECTED MINUTES, summed. It is not minutes-share and it never was. It also goes one better than this row asks by pricing against a stand_in that blends bench quality with replacement level at ABSORPTION 0.50, so an absence costs what her actual replacement costs rather than her full value. It SUPERSEDES ops/analytics/availability_v3.py, which carries the same functions and predates three fixes that changed the answer: the identity gate, garbage-time exclusion, and walk-forward fitting. This is the built-but-never-wired pattern again, and it is the actual reason the margin number prices absence at zero, which this row opens by observing. SO THE QUESTION IS NOT HOW TO BUILD IT. It fired 14 times today and published twice, both after the non-fast-forward that had frozen the public repo was repaired. So the reader sees a board roughly twenty minutes stale rather than a frozen one, and the lightweight refresh keeps generated_utc moving - but the full bake has not completed since last night. ONE MEASURED LEAD, NOT A DIAGNOSIS: the failures begin at 22:49 on 08-19, the first pass after the last success, and the ops_monitor lines through that window read width=5/2, width=6/3 and width=10/3 - five to ten lanes against an authorised three on a four-core box. A bake that fits in 179 seconds idle does not fit in 420 under that load. Whoever takes this should measure the bake's runtime against concurrent lane count BEFORE touching another timeout constant - the constants were already cut once today on a task-limit theory that measurement disproved. || THE LEAD THIS ROW ASKED FOR IS NOW MEASURED, and it is not lane count. 2026-08-20T08:06Z: CPU load read 100 percent on six consecutive samples over 24 seconds on a FOUR-CORE box. Live per-process share at that moment: chrome 25 percent, then three python processes at 20, 19 and 14 - over half the machine - plus a second chrome at 5. EIGHT python processes were running concurrently, all Hardwood: build_site --push (the bake itself, trying to run), daily_reconcile --run, board_selfpolice, report_scheduler --tick, bluesky_extract --write, discord_gateway_listener --run, slack_ceo_current --run and stale_done_check. SO THE CONSTANTS WERE NEVER THE DEFECT. A 240-second budget for a bake that is getting a fraction of one core is not miscalibration, it is an oversubscribed box, and lengthening the budget only moves where the kill lands - which is exactly what the 420-second era showed. Corroborating evidence from the same window: the 07:55:07 pass logged 'bake+push DEFERRED rc=75 - the box was busy' from the heavy-job admission gate, and the lightweight refresh immediately after it raised TimeoutExpired. The admission gate is working correctly; it is deferring into a machine that never becomes free. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY MOVE IT, in rough order of leverage and none of it done here: stagger the scheduled tasks so the bake does not overlap daily_reconcile and report_scheduler; give the bake a real priority claim rather than an equal share; and note that roughly 30 percent of the box is Chrome, which is the CEO's browser and not ours to touch but is part of the honest picture. The two long-lived listeners, discord_gateway and slack_ceo, are cheap individually and permanent, so they are a floor rather than a spike. ONE MEASUREMENT NOT TAKEN: how long the bake needs on an idle box. That is the number that would turn this from a diagnosis into a budget, and it cannot be taken while the box is at 100 percent. || THE MISSING NUMBER, caught in flight 2026-08-20T08:31Z. A build_site holding an admission slot since 08:21:29 had consumed 163 CPU-SECONDS over 570 wall-clock seconds - about 29 percent of one core, roughly 7 percent of the four-core box. So the bake wants on the order of three CPU-minutes and is being handed a quarter of a core, which is why it takes ten wall-clock minutes and why every 240-second budget kills it mid-flight. That is the budget question answered without needing an idle box: the work is about three minutes; the wall clock is a function of how much machine it gets. ALSO WORTH RECORDING: the admission gate is slot-based, not load-based - two slots on this box - and at 08:31 only ONE was held. So the gate is not the thing wedging the pipeline; it defers only when both slots are genuinely taken, and its own starvation warning already names the two possibilities. The pipeline is not deadlocked, it is slow, and it is slow because the box is oversubscribed. || THE BIGGEST NAMED COMPETITOR, measured 2026-08-20T09:07Z. The admission gate's holder at that moment was bluesky_extract, pid 10548, HOLDING A HEAVY SLOT FOR 1,403 SECONDS - twenty-three minutes. It is not wedged: sampling its CPU twelve seconds apart gave 557.8 then 565.1 seconds, so it is consuming about 61 percent of one core and genuinely working. Total 565 CPU-seconds in 23 minutes of wall clock. On a two-slot gate and a four-core box, one job of that size plus the bake plus the browser is the saturation, and it is why the 08:58:46 bake+push was DEFERRED as busy sixty seconds after it started. SO THE STARVATION HAS A NAME NOW, and the gate's own warning offers the two options: either a holder is wedged below the TTL, which this one is not, or the slot count is too small for the real workload. A third option the warning does not list is that a twenty-three-minute job should not be competing for the same two slots as the sixty-second board bake at all. Whether bluesky_extract runs less often, runs bounded, or runs outside the heavy gate is an ops call, but it is the specific thing to look at rather than another timeout constant. || THE SLOT HOLDER IS AN ORPHAN, and this is the sharpest version of the diagnosis so far. HardwoodBluesky carries ExecutionTimeLimit PT9M. Its child, bluesky_extract.py --write at pid 10548, started 08:43Z and was still running at 09:20 with 829 CPU-seconds - thirty-six minutes, four times its own limit - while Task Scheduler reported LastTaskResult 0 for a NEWER run started at 09:01. The limit killed a wrapper and the child outlived it. It holds one of the gate's two heavy slots the entire time at about 61 percent of a core, which is exactly why the 08:58:46 bake was deferred as busy a minute after starting. Filed as its own row: a-nine-minute-task-has-been-running-thirty-six-minutes-holding-the-bake-out. SO THE ORDER OF THE FIX IS NOW CLEAR, and it is not the timeouts. First stop a nine-minute task from running thirty-six minutes. Then decide whether a job of that shape shares a two-slot gate with a sixty-second board bake. Only after both does any timeout constant here mean anything, because until then the bake is bidding for a quarter of a core against a job that will not release.

infra.status: open - premise confirmed and both obvious fixes eliminated with evidence; the console-window probe is the untested direction ||| THE THIRD APPROACH IS NOW TESTED AND IT WORKS, 2026-08-07T12:53Z, with both controls. AttachConsole(pid) followed by GetConsoleWindow discriminates cleanly. POSITIVE control, this genuinely visible coordinator pid 12808: Attached True, ConsoleWindow 2097290, non-zero. NEGATIVE control, the headless pythonw scout pid 10592: Attached FALSE, ConsoleWindow 0. So the probe separates a console-hosted head from a headless one where MainWindowHandle and the ancestor walk both failed. 🔴 IMPLEMENTATION LANDMINE THAT WOULD BREAK THE VISIBILITY LAW ITSELF: AttachConsole DETACHES THE CALLING PROCESS FROM ITS OWN CONSOLE. hardwood_supervisor.ps1 RENDERS the console the CEO watches, so calling this probe inside the supervisor process would tear down the very window the law exists to protect. THE PROBE MUST RUN IN A SHORT-LIVED SUBPROCESS and report back a boolean. I used FreeConsole around it here for exactly that reason and this session still has its window. HONEST LIMIT ON THE EVIDENCE: this is proven against a real headless control, pythonw with no console at all. It is NOT proven against the specific bg-pty-host case the parent row is about, because no such process exists on the box right now to test. A pty-host may attach a PSEUDOconsole and behave differently. Strong evidence, not the exact case - verify against a real bg-pty-host head before shipping. RE-CONFIRMED 2026-08-12 ON A DIFFERENT LIVE HEAD - THE DESTRUCTIVE FINDING REPRODUCES EXACTLY. This row measured claude.exe pid 12808 with MainWindowHandle ZERO. I measured THIS session, pid 10632 - the pid coordinator_lock granted me at claim, in a window the CEO is looking at right now - and it has MainWindowHandle 0 and an EMPTY TITLE. So does every conhost on the box, in session 0 and session 1 alike. The only process holding a real handle is WindowsTerminal pid 1048, session 1, handle 1442740, AND ITS TITLE IS 'claude'. SO FIX ONE WOULD HAVE REAPED ME. A MainWindowHandle test on the coordinator process marks a genuinely visible head invisible, and under the VISIBILITY LAW a head that fails the visible test is killed and relaunched. Two independent sessions five days apart now show the same zero, so this is the normal state of a visible coordinator here and not a quirk of one launch. AND FIX TWO IS CONFIRMED USELESS FOR THE STATED REASON: the window does not belong to claude.exe at all, it belongs to WindowsTerminal, which hosts through a broker and is therefore NOT an ancestor. No parent walk can reach it. ONE CONSTRUCTIVE OBSERVATION, offered as a lead rather than a fix: the terminal that owns the window CARRIES THE COORDINATOR'S NAME in its title. That is a real signal a probe could use - but it is machine-wide rather than per-pid, so it would pass a pipe-backed head whenever any real terminal happens to be open, which is most of the time. It is a corroborator, never the test. WHY I DID NOT TEST THE THIRD DIRECTION, and it is a genuine hazard rather than caution: this row's untested idea is a per-pid console probe via attach. ATTACHING A CONSOLE FROM INSIDE THE LIVE COORDINATOR'S OWN TOOLING RISKS DISTURBING THE SESSION UNDER TEST - the one head on the box, in the window the CEO watches. That probe wants writing as a standalone script and running against a DELIBERATELY SPAWNED throwaway head, one visible and one pipe-backed, so it can be shown to discriminate before anything acts on its verdict. THE THIRD DIRECTION IS BUILT AND IT DISCRIMINATES - ops/scout/console_visibility_probe.py, 2026-08-12. This row named a per-pid console probe as the untested idea that might work. It works. MEASURED ON LIVE PROCESSES: pid 10632, THIS coordinator, in the window the CEO watches - has_console true, hwnd 918932, visible true, EXIT 0 VISIBLE. pid 11776, the interactive supervisor in session 1 - has_console true, hwnd 263360, visible true, EXIT 0. pid 1048, WindowsTerminal - no console, exit 1, which is correct because it HOSTS a console rather than owning one and is not a coordinator. A nonexistent pid returns err 87 and exit 1. SO IT GETS RIGHT EXACTLY WHAT MainWindowHandle GOT WRONG: both genuinely visible session-1 processes read VISIBLE here and read INVISIBLE under the handle test. That is the destructive direction closed - the failure that reaps a live head is a FALSE NEGATIVE, and the probe produces none on the two live heads available to test. WHAT IS STILL UNTESTED, STATED PLAINLY: the NEGATIVE side. A pipe-backed head should return has_console false, and I had none to point it at - there is one head on this box and it is visible. So this is proven not to reap a live head, and NOT yet proven to catch a headless one. Both halves matter and only one is done. Spawn a deliberate pipe-backed throwaway and re-run before wiring the verdict to any action. THREE PROPERTIES BUILT IN ON PURPOSE. It runs as a SUBPROCESS and says why in its own docstring: AttachConsole rebinds the CALLING process's console, so calling it in-process would rebind the console of the only live head. It FreeConsole()s first, or a target that does own a console reads as one that does not. And EXIT 2 IS UNKNOWN, distinct from exit 1 invisible - which earned itself immediately: my first draft looked GetConsoleWindow up on user32 instead of kernel32 and raised AttributeError, and the probe returned 2 rather than 'invisible'. A caller acting on that would have REFUSED TO REAP on a typo instead of killing a healthy coordinator. That is the fail-safe direction working before the code was even correct.

infra.status: ready MEASURED 2026-08-12 - THE SIGNAL THIS FIX NEEDS ALREADY EXISTS AND RUNS, AND NOTHING IN THE ALARM PATH ASKS IT. RERANKED p2 WITH THE FIX FULLY SPECIFIED. THE PROVIDER SIGNAL IS BUILT: ops/deploy_watch.py carries provider_status(), polling https://www.githubstatus.com/api/v2/summary.json until Actions AND Pages read operational. It exists precisely because of the outage this row is about, and it runs - HardwoodDeployWatch is a registered scheduled task, Ready, S4U, confirmed in the task store tonight. BUT NOTHING CONSULTS IT FROM THE ALARM PATH. grep across ops and scripts finds exactly two mentions of deploy_watch outside the module: a comment in ops/scout/preflight.py about the gh token, and a note in unwired_capability_check.py that the module is the Arguments of its scheduled task. NO CALLER of provider_status anywhere. So the machine knows the provider is down and the card still says our repair failed. A DESIGN CONSTRAINT THE FIX MUST RESPECT, and it is why the obvious approach would be rejected: these CRITICAL cards are PINNED PLAIN LINES on purpose. ops/notify.py says so at the publish_stale entry - pin plain CEO-safe lines so no stamp, lag-seconds or job id can ride the push, the board carries the detail. So the fix is NOT caller-supplied text explaining the outage; that is exactly what the pinning bans. THE FIX, SPECIFIED: add a SECOND pinned line for the upstream case - something like, the public site is not refreshing because the hosting provider is having an outage, our content is ready and will publish when they recover - and have the publish_stale path select between the two by calling deploy_watch.provider_status() at alarm time. Same pinning discipline, correct attribution. Mind the comms-gate send-blockers when wording it: no SQL-verb update, no the word blocked, no version tokens. WHY IT IS p2 AND NOT DONE TONIGHT: this changes what reaches the CEO's phone, on a path whose whole design is that nothing free-form gets there. That is worth doing deliberately rather than at the end of a long session. THE TRIGGERING OUTAGE IS OVER - Pages has five consecutive successful deploys today, newest 09:14:31Z - so nothing is currently mis-attributing, and the next outage is the deadline rather than today.

The defect is exactly as filed and it is still in the code. ops/ops_consultant_scheduler.py run_once stamps last_fired_utc immediately after build_evidence and drop_work_item - that is when the digest is REQUESTED, not when one is WRITTEN - so a fire that produces nothing advances the clock and is indistinguishable from one that succeeded. A separate mark_fired path exists with the correct delivery-time contract, but the fire path stamps regardless, so the correct path does not protect the wrong one. THE DROUGHT DID BREAK, which is worth recording because it changes the urgency rather than the defect: digests run 20260723, 24, 29, 31 and then jump to 20260811. So the gap was ELEVEN days, longer than the six this row measured on 08-06, and it ended on its own. Today's is real, 6544 bytes. FIXED THE MEASUREMENT, NOT THE CADENCE. Added newest_digest and _digest_lines: --status now prints the newest digest ACTUALLY ON DISK beside the clock, and emits a loud DIVERGENCE line when the clock last fired more than a day after the newest digest was written. Live output today reads last fired 2026-08-11T19:47:06Z and last DIGEST ON DISK 2026-08-11, 1.4d ago, no divergence - which is the correct quiet state. PROVEN TO BITE BY REPLAYING THE FAILURE: fed the 2026-08-06 state, clock fired 08-06 with the newest digest at 07-31, it prints DIVERGENCE, the clock last fired 6.5d AFTER the newest digest was written. The empty case prints last DIGEST ON DISK none found, the clock above is a REQUEST time, not proof. So the exact silence this row describes is now visible on the surface that misreported it as 24.2 hours. CADENCE CONTROL FLOW IS DELIBERATELY UNTOUCHED. Making the scheduler refuse to fire while digests are missing would make it go quiet exactly when it is most needed - the same over-eager-guard trap as the apply-first gate. The clock still drives firing; it just can no longer claim to be evidence of delivery.
